title: Consumer Spending in Canada Is Shifting, Just Not How You’d Expect
gist: BCG argues Canadian consumer growth has been financed by savings drawdown, asset gains, and debt rather than real income, and that as budgets tighten the essential/discretionary and premium/value labels stop predicting category resilience. The actionable map is income divergence per category — Dining, Alcohol, Apparel and DIY are becoming release valves while Pet Care, Automotive, Leisure Travel and Beauty are being protected — and the proof-of-value that closes a sale differs by income cohort and purchase stakes.

insights.claim: Recent Canadian consumer spending growth has been funded by savings drawdown, asset valuation gains, and debt rather than by real income growth, which continues to lag.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Canadian consumer-facing revenue lines rest on a wealth-and-credit foundation, so a housing or credit shock hits retail demand faster than wage data would suggest — watch Canadian household savings rate and debt service ratios as the leading indicator, not employment.
insights.quote: Much of the country’s recent consumer growth has been borrowed, sustained by savings, asset valuation gains, and debt as real incomes lag.
insights.locator: Financial pressure is rewriting the hierarchy

insights.claim: Under budget pressure Canadian households are not cutting proportionally across discretionary spending; they defend certain discretionary categories and use others as release valves to absorb the squeeze.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Screening consumer names by an essential-vs-discretionary bucket will mis-rank downside risk; the release-valve categories carry the concentrated earnings cuts.
insights.quote: They are protecting some discretionary spending while using other areas as release valves.
insights.locator: Yet as budgets tighten, households are not

insights.claim: In some major retail categories higher-income households spend two to four times what lower-income households spend, while in other categories spending is close to even — so income skew, not the essential/discretionary label, defines a category's exposure.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Build a per-category income-skew score for consumer holdings; a high-skew retailer is a play on asset-price-driven upper-income spending, a low-skew one on real wages.
insights.quote: Higher-income households spend two to four times as much as lower-income households in some major retail categories. In others, spending is close to even.

insights.claim: Household appliances, a large discretionary ticket, show relatively little income divergence, while pet care — usually treated as a resilient everyday staple — is skewed toward higher earners trading up to premium options.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Pet care's defensive reputation is partly a premiumization story dependent on affluent buyers, so premium pet names are more cyclical than the staples multiple implies; big-ticket appliance demand is broader-based than feared.
insights.quote: Pet Care, often treated as a resilient everyday expense, is more nuanced with higher earners more willing to trade-up to premium options.
insights.locator: Household Appliances, a large discretionary purchase

insights.claim: Mobile technology and mobile service plans display different income-divergence patterns despite serving closely related use cases, showing that adjacent categories in the same consumer need can decouple in resilience.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Handset retail and connectivity subscriptions should be underwritten separately — device upgrade cycles and ARPU trends will not move together through a consumer squeeze.
insights.locator: Mobile Technology and Mobile Service Plans also follow

themes.theme: Six-month intent as the divergence signal

insights.claim: Six-month spending intentions in Canada remain positive for pet care, automotive, leisure travel, and beauty, while weakening for dining, alcohol, apparel, and DIY home improvement — identifying the categories households are protecting versus using to make room.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: A ready-made pairs setup for Canadian consumer exposure: long protected categories (pet, auto, travel, beauty) against the release valves (restaurants, alcohol, apparel, home improvement).
insights.quote: Spending intent remains positive in Pet Care, Automotive, Leisure Travel, and Beauty, while weakening in Dining, Alcohol, Apparel, and DIY Home Improvement.
insights.locator: The pattern reveals which categories lower-income

insights.claim: The most consequential shifts are starting in categories that still look income-balanced today — fresh food and staples, mobile service plans, DIY home improvement, leisure travel, and alcoholic beverages — where higher- and lower-income households are only beginning to move apart.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Current spend data will look calm in exactly the categories about to bifurcate — intent surveys, not trailing sales, are the early-warning instrument here.
insights.quote: Some of the most consequential movements occur in categories that look broadly balanced today.
insights.locator: Spending Intentions Show Where Demand Is Starting to Diverge

insights.claim: Divergence takes two distinct forms: in dining lower-income households are pulling back while higher-income households intend to spend more, whereas in automotive and beauty both groups intend to spend more but higher earners are accelerating faster.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Distinguish absolute-loss categories like dining, where low-income volume disappears, from relative-mix categories like auto and beauty, where the whole category still grows but the premium tier compounds faster.
insights.quote: In Dining, lower-income households are pulling back while higher-income households intend to spend more.
insights.locator: The divergence is taking different forms

insights.claim: The standard retail reflex of deeper promotion works only for frequent low-risk purchases; for expensive infrequent items, lower-income buyers become especially sensitive to reliability because a bad decision is harder to absorb, so reassurance rather than discount is the binding constraint.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Retailers responding to a consumer squeeze with blanket markdowns will burn margin without converting big-ticket demand — treat heavy promo intensity in durables as a warning, not a share-gain story.
insights.quote: Promotions lose force when the product itself falls short.
insights.locator: This complicates the usual response to financial pressure

insights.claim: Proof of value splits by cohort: in household appliances lower-income buyers weight brand reputation and trust, while higher-income buyers weight service and the buying experience, and for low-stakes frequent purchases lower earners optimize quantity-per-dollar while higher earners weight durability and functionality.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Brand equity is the moat in the lower-income durables segment and service infrastructure is the moat in the higher-income one — capex on white-glove delivery and installation only pays where the customer base has already skewed up.
insights.locator: Buyers Demand Different Proof of Value

insights.claim: The recommended retail response is four capability shifts — a good-better-best range architecture anchored by own-brand sourcing, cohort-intelligent pricing and promotion, loyalty redesigned by cohort (cashback and volume rewards for lower earners, service upgrades and perks for higher earners), and reallocating SKUs and investment toward each cohort's preferred banner and channel.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: A concrete checklist for judging which listed retailers are positioned for a K-shaped consumer: private-label depth, promo/pricing systems, tiered loyalty, and banner-level capital allocation.
insights.quote: A one-size loyalty program underserves both groups.
insights.locator: What This Means for Retail Leaders

insights.claim: Where the direction of a category's demand is still unsettled, retaining strategic flexibility is worth more than committing capital early to either the value or the premium end of the market.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Optionality has explicit value in this cycle — penalize retailers making large irreversible bets on one income tier before the divergence resolves.
insights.quote: Where the direction of demand remains unsettled, preserving flexibility may be more valuable than committing early to one part of the market.
insights.locator: Where the direction of demand remains unsettled

insights.claim: Planning around a single average consumer is the core strategic error in a K-shaped economy, because the income divide demands a different response in every category rather than one company-wide posture.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Aggregate consumer-confidence and average-basket data are losing forecasting power; the tradeable dispersion is inside the consumer sector, between cohort-aligned winners and average-consumer laggards.
insights.quote: The income divide doesn't call for a single strategic response - it calls for a different one in every category.
